1.pericope_label: We then, as workers together with him, beseech you also that ye receive not the grace of God in vain

schools.summary: Set out the possibilities for the participle, which may mean either that the apostles were joint labourers with one another in entreating, or that they co-operated with God in securing the reconciliation of the world; note the older English renderings, one giving simply helpers and another the joint-labourers of God, and report the scholar who supposes the word to be in the vocative and an address to fellow-labourers — adding that in this opinion he is probably alone and has manifestly departed from the scope and design of the passage. Grant elsewhere that the unexpressed pronoun may grammatically be referred either to God or to Christ, but decide for the former on the general tone of the context and the apostle’s language in other epistles. Say shortly that we are co-workers and partners with God in this work of grace. Take the grace of God to mean the gracious offer of reconciliation and pardon, and the entreaty to mean that this offer must not be neglected or slighted so as to lose the benefit of it: it is offered freely and fully and all may be saved, but it may also be slighted, and men may hear of a Saviour and have the offers of mercy pressed on them and all be in vain — for simply to hear of the plan of salvation will no more save a sinner than to hear of medicine will save the sick, since it must be embraced and applied. Observe that these words were probably addressed to professors of religion, who are therefore to use all possible care lest the offers have been made in vain, examining their own hearts, inquiring into their condition and guarding against self-deception. Press the same on the baptised: those written to had believed and been baptised and so had received the grace, but the freedom of the will to choose good or evil remained, and if they chose evil they would frustrate the end which the grace was intended to work out. And give the closing phrase its literal force, into emptiness, since the plan of God, the work of Christ on the cross and the pleas of the ambassador may all be nullified by the recipient of the message.

Note that the ministers of the gospel are workers or labourers, that their ministry is a work and a very laborious one which none have strength for of themselves, and that it requires faithfulness and diligence and is honourable; and that they do not work alone, being fellow workers subordinate to Christ, who is the chief shepherd where they are under ones and the chief master builder where they are under workers, so that his being with them is their honour and the reason their work succeeds. Observe that the phrase rendered with him is not in the original text, where one word only is used, and that it may be rendered fellow workers or fellow labourers, meaning with one another. Then explain what the co-working is: after the instructions of the embassy have been faithfully communicated, the ministers must also use their endeavour that these may be carried into effect, adding continual exhortations so that the embassy may be efficacious and their labour not in vain — for it is not enough to deliver a message if one does not also press it, and the doctrine of the gospel is helped by exhortations so as not to be without effect, ministers connecting their endeavours with God’s commission as it is the part of an ambassador to enforce by arguments what he brings forward in the name of his prince. Allow that the particle may relate to God, or to the embassy assigned to his servants, or to the endeavours of ministers in common.

Give the errand itself first, that being favoured with the gospel they should not receive this grace of God in vain: the gospel is a word of grace sounding in our ears, but it will be in vain for us to hear it unless we believe it and comply with the end and design of it. Note that since it is the duty of the ministers of the gospel to exhort and persuade their hearers to accept the grace and mercy offered them, they are honoured with the high title of co-workers with God — yet observe the limits: they must work, and work for God and his glory and for souls and their good, and they are workers with God and yet under him, as instruments only; but if they be faithful they may hope to find God working with them, and their labour will be effectual. Then mark the language and way of the spirit of the gospel, which is not roughness and severity but all mildness and gentleness, beseeching and entreating, using exhortations and arguments in order to prevail with sinners and overcome their natural unwillingness to be reconciled to God and to be happy for ever.

Give the argument of the chapter in order before beginning, from the warning not to receive the grace of God in vain, through the care to bring no disgrace on the gospel, the account of how the apostles behaved and suffered and rejoiced, the affectionate concern for the readers, the counsel against being yoked with unbelievers and the arguments for avoiding them, to the exhortation to avoid evil company on the promise of adoption. Then say plainly that the last two words of the opening clause are not in the text: some supply with you, and one ancient version seems to have read so, but no manuscript has this reading and no other version; and for your own part see nothing wanting if the word apostles is supplied, so that we, being fellow workers, also entreat you. Identify the grace of God as the grand sacrificial offering of Christ for the sin of the world, just before mentioned in speaking of the ministry of reconciliation. And elsewhere refer the fellow-labouring to the hearers themselves, who are working out their own salvation, adding that we receive the grace by faith, and not in vain if we add to this a persevering holiness.

Ask why the warning follows so closely on the entreaty, and answer that since he had said God beseeches and that ambassadors and suppliants are sent, they might become supine on the strength of it; so he here again alarms and arouses them, saying that we entreat you not to receive the grace of God in vain — let us not therefore be at ease because he beseeches and has sent some to be ambassadors, but for that very reason let us make haste to please God and to collect spiritual merchandise, that we may not after so much affectionate care, by being supine and exhibiting no nobleness, miss such great blessings. Set a term to the beseeching: do not, because he has sent some to exhort you, deem that this will always be so, for it will be so until his second coming and so long as we are here, but after that is judgment and punishment. And press the shortness of the remaining time as an argument of its own, as elsewhere it is said that now is our salvation nearer, and that the Lord is at hand.

Expound the earthly dwelling-place of the previous chapter: when it is said that we have an eternal home in heaven not made with hands, it is by no means implied that because our present house was built by the Creator’s hand it must perish in a perpetual dissolution after death; the subject is treated in order to offer consolation against the fear of death and the dread of that very dissolution. Argue it from what follows, that in this tabernacle we groan, earnestly desiring to be clothed upon with the vesture which is from heaven, so that having been unclothed we shall not be found naked — that is, shall regain that of which we have been divested, even our body. And connect it with the earlier epistle, where the dead shall be raised incorruptible, meaning those who had undergone mortality, and we shall be changed, meaning those whom God shall find yet in the flesh: both shall be raised incorruptible, because they shall regain their body, and that a renewed one, from which their incorruptibility shall come.

debates: Whom the workers are working together with.
Whether the unexpressed pronoun refers to God, to Christ, to one another, or to the hearers.
What the co-working of a minister actually consists in.
Who is addressed by the warning against receiving grace in vain.
How long the season of entreaty lasts.
outliers: Five different referents are supplied for one pronoun that is not in the Greek at all.
Barnes reports a commentator who takes the participle as a vocative, and says he is probably alone in it.
Clarke notes that one ancient version appears to read with you, though no manuscript supports it.
Ellicott presses the warning on the already baptised, on the ground that the will remains free after grace is received.
Chrysostom fixes a term to the ministry of entreaty at the second coming.
Two of the blocks printed at this verse expound the previous chapter rather than this one.

2.pericope_label: Behold, now is the accepted time; behold, now is the day of salvation — giving no offence in any thing, that the ministry be not blamed

schools.summary: Note that the quotation interrupts the sentence, the participial construction of the following verse being resumed from the one before, and call it another of the apostle’s parentheses. State the principle of citation frankly: the words are quoted not as affirming that they are used in exactly the sense, or with reference to the same design, for which they were originally spoken, but as expressing the idea the writer wished to convey, or in accordance with the general principle implied in their first use — the general idea there being that under the Messiah God would be willing to hear and disposed to show mercy to Jew and Gentile alike, and the doctrine here that in Christ God is willing to show mercy now. Assume that the writer had the whole context in mind as well as the words cited, and recall that they were addressed first to the servant of the Lord as the light of the Gentiles and then, in his name, to the nation. Observe that where the older version has the simple verbal the apostle employs a double compound meaning well-received, and that the second word for accepted is much stronger than the first, entirely acceptable being perhaps its best equivalent; and suggest that the solemnity of the sentence may have been intensified by what seemed the nearness of the impending judgment, opportunities being offered which might never again recur. On the following verse, take the word rendered offence as properly a stumbling, and make the point institutional: it is not that one man would be reproached, but that the ministry itself, which the Lord had established, would be reproached by the misconduct of any one engaged in it, since the misconduct of one preacher brings reproach on the profession and prevents the usefulness and success of others. Hear a subtle distinction in the two forms of the Greek negative, suggesting that the writer is giving his own estimate of his aim and endeavour, avoiding all occasion of offence not because he fears censure for himself but that the ministry be not blamed. And note that the noun stands here alone in the New Testament and that the Greek doubles its negative.

Take the person addressed in the prophecy to be Christ, and enumerate the hearings: he was heard when he prayed for his own glorification, being strengthened as man in his work, raised from the dead and set at the Father’s right hand; he was heard in the garden, where the will of God was done according to his desire and he was delivered from the fear of death; and he was heard on the cross. Make the fit turn on a relation rather than on a text: it is without doubt of the kingdom of Christ that the prophet speaks, the Father appointing his Son a leader for the purpose of gathering a Church; and since we know what correspondence there is between the Head and the members, and since Christ was heard in our name, the salvation of all of us being entrusted to his hand, we are all admonished in his person not to slight the opportunity afforded for obtaining salvation. Then read the following verse as the apostle’s account of himself and his colleagues, who knew that men were waiting to vilify the ministry of the word and hinder its progress, and who therefore took all possible care to lay no stumbling-block before hearer or reader, Jew or Gentile, whether by word or writing, by doctrine or conversation. And set the passage in the quarrel: the writer sometimes commends the ministry of the gospel generally and at other times his own integrity, and here he sets before us in his own person a living picture of a good and faithful apostle, that the Corinthians may see how unfair they were in preferring empty blusterers before him, assigning the praise to mere pretences and holding in the highest esteem persons effeminate and devoid of zeal — the very things he mentions to his own commendation having probably been brought forward by them as grounds of contempt.

Show that the citation follows the Greek version word for word and letter for letter, and give the two Hebrew phrases behind it, the time of God’s pleasure or benevolence, of which all the faithful were in expectation, and the day of salvation, the time when that salvation should be manifested and applied; then argue that the ministry of reconciliation being now exercised in full force is itself the proof that the prophecy is fulfilled, so that now the Messiah reigns, now is the gospel dispensation, and now is the very time in which the power of God is present to heal and every sinner believing may be saved. Propose a re-ordering of the text: this second verse should be read immediately after the last verse of the preceding chapter, since where it now stands it greatly disturbs the connection between the verses on either side of it — and set the whole passage down in the order it should stand. On the following verse, take the word rendered offence as a stumbling-block in general, or anything over which a man stumbles or falls, and here as any transgression or scandal occurring among the ministers or the Christians themselves by which Jews or Gentiles might take occasion of offence and vilify the gospel of Christ. And reduce the whole to a proportion: as of old there was a particular time wherein God was pleased to pour out his peculiar blessing, so there is now, and this is that time, a time of peculiar blessing; giving, so far as in us lies, no offence, that the ministry be not blamed on our account.

Preach the verse to catechumens as the season of confession: confess what you have done in word or in deed, by night or by day; confess in an acceptable time, and in the day of salvation receive the heavenly treasure. Devote your time to the exorcisms and be assiduous at the catechisings, remembering the things spoken, for they are spoken not for your ears only but that by faith you may seal them up in the memory. Blot out from your mind all earthly care, for you are running for your soul; you are utterly forsaking the things of the world, and little are the things you forsake beside what the Lord is giving. Forsake things present and put your trust in things to come. Having run so many circles of the years busied in vain about the world, have you not forty days to be free for prayer, for your own soul’s sake? Excuse yourself from talking many idle words, neither backbite nor lend a willing ear to backbiters, but rather be prompt to prayer.

debates: Where the quoted verse belongs in the argument.
In what sense the apostle uses the prophet’s words.
Who is addressed in the prophecy.
Why the apostle strengthens the word he found in his source.
Whose reputation is protected by giving no offence.
outliers: Clarke would move the quoted verse to the end of the previous chapter; Ellicott and Robertson merely call it a parenthesis.
Barnes states outright that the apostle does not use the prophet in the sense for which the words were first spoken.
Robertson, Ellicott and the editorial matter printed with Calvin all notice independently that the apostle strengthens the word of the Greek version.
Cyril of Jerusalem applies the verse to the forty days of preparation and the discipline of catechumens.
Calvin reads the following verses as a self-portrait answering readers who preferred showier teachers.
Barnes makes the offence a danger to the institution of the ministry rather than to one man’s name.

4.pericope_label: But in all things approving ourselves as the ministers of God, in much patience, in afflictions, in necessities, in distresses, in stripes, in imprisonments, in tumults

schools.summary: Map the catalogue before entering it: here is a marvellous summary of the argument about the dignity and glory of ministers of Christ, under three aspects, the first governed by in, the second by by, the third by as, with the negative view stated first and the positive following; and observe that each word carries a story that can be filled in from the writer’s own life, with an echo in that of us all. Keep up the connection with the earlier passages about self-commendation, and hear the writer harping on the phrase: yes, he does commend himself, but by acts and not by words, looking back on a life of labour and sufferings and challenging comparison with those who carry letters of commendation; note that the Greek has the word ministers in the nominative where the English suggests the objective, and that what follows was likely to expose him to a repetition of the cynical sneer, of which his generous indignation makes him nobly regardless. Say elsewhere, more simply, that the aim was to live as was appropriate to the ministers of God and so commend the ministry to the confidence and affection of men, and that a minister who murmured when poor or persecuted or imprisoned would do little good by all his preaching, God placing his ministers in peculiar trial partly that they may illustrate their own precepts by example. Correct the word rendered patience to endurance, which is much stronger than the English. Give the root-ideas of the opening triad in order — being pressed upon, a constraint that leaves no choice of action, being so hemmed in that no way is open — while allowing that the words may have been used without formal classification; and translate the third as tight places. Then locate the particulars in the history: the scourging and the imprisonment at Philippi, with other instances implied elsewhere, and tumults at Antioch in Pisidia, Lystra, Thessalonica, Corinth and Ephesus. Take the word for tumults as instabilities, often arising from politics; render the watchings as sleeplessnesses, instances of insomnia; and refer both watchings and fastings to voluntary acts, nights of vigil and self-imposed abstinence, rather than to privations incidental to the work.

Say that it is not enough for a minister of the gospel to avoid whatever might bring blot or scandal on his ministry, but that he should in all things, and by all lawful and laudable means, approve and show himself a true and faithful dispenser of the word. Then explain what the whole enumeration is for: it shows that all the tests by which the Lord is accustomed to try his servants were to be found in this man, and that there was no kind of test to which he had not been subjected, in order that the faithfulness of his ministry might be the more fully established. Draw a distinction within the list: some things enumerated are under all circumstances required of all the servants of Christ, while others are not necessary in all cases, since a man need not be put to the test by stripes and imprisonments in order to be a servant of Christ, and these will in some cases be wanting in the experience of the best — though it becomes all to be of such a disposition as to present themselves to be so tried, if the Lord shall see fit. Define the patience as the regulation of the mind in adversity, an excellence that ought invariably to distinguish a good minister. And on the tumults, locate the praise exactly: it does not consist in his being unmoved by them, since that is commonly found among all riotous persons, but in his being thrown into no alarm by tumults stirred up through the fault of others, so that in proportion to the calmness of his disposition was the greater excellence displayed in standing undaunted. Two things are required of ministers of the gospel, that they endeavour to the utmost of their power to maintain peace, and yet go forward undaunted through the midst of commotions, so as not to turn aside from the right course though heaven and earth should be mingled. Report also the other understanding of the word, as the inconvenience of being frequently compelled to change country because he was left in peace nowhere. And count the beatings, thrice with rods and five times with the scourge of forty save one.

Show how conscientiously the work was done, since they not only gave no offence in anything but laboured to manifest themselves the genuine ministers of God, bearing calmly up under the most painful and oppressive afflictions. Distinguish the triad: the first may signify the series of persecutions and distresses in general, the state of cruel suffering in which the Church and the apostles then existed; the second, straits and difficulties, including all the want that arose from the impoverished state of the Church; the third, such straits as were absolutely unavoidable and insurmountable, the word implying a man reduced to a narrow place and driven into a corner, hemmed in on every side as the Israelites were at the Red Sea, the sea before them, Pharaoh and his host behind them and Egyptian fortresses on either hand, so that God alone could bring them out when their enemies saw that the wilderness had shut them in. Elsewhere make the same three a gradation of hope: in afflictions several ways to escape may appear, though none without difficulty; in necessities one only, and that a difficult one; in distresses none at all appears. Take the tumults as insurrections raised against them because of the gospel, which is more natural than understanding the word of agitations or tossings to and fro from place to place, and describe them as attacks a man cannot stand against but which bear him hither and thither by violence. Take the labours both of working with their own hands to provide the necessaries of life, that they might not be chargeable to others, and of spreading the gospel wherever providence opened the way; the watchings of passing many nights without sleep or rest; and the fastings as partly constrained through want of food and partly voluntary, as a means of obtaining an increase of grace both for themselves and for the churches.

debates: How the catalogue of the following verses is arranged.
How a minister commends himself without self-commendation.
What the three opening words of the list distinguish.
Whether all these trials are required of every servant of Christ.
Whether the fastings and watchings were voluntary or forced.
outliers: Robertson divides the whole passage by its three governing prepositions.
Wesley reads the opening triad as a descending scale of possible escapes.
Clarke illustrates the third term from Israel hemmed in at the Red Sea.
Calvin distinguishes the trials required of every minister from those merely to be accepted if sent.
Ellicott makes both watchings and fastings voluntary; Clarke divides the fastings between want and choice.
Calvin locates the praise not in bearing tumults but in bearing tumults raised by other men’s fault.

6.pericope_label: By pureness, by knowledge, by longsuffering, by kindness, by the Holy Ghost, by love unfeigned — by the armour of righteousness on the right hand and on the left, by honour and dishonour

schools.summary: Narrow the first word: it may possibly mean purity of motive in the widest sense, but the use of the corresponding adjective elsewhere is decisive in favour of purity from sensual sin, that is personal chastity — and in the general state of morals throughout the empire, and writing to such a city as this, it was natural to dwell on that aspect of the Christian character. Elsewhere take it more widely as integrity and sanctity and a holy life, observing that all preaching would be in vain without it, that one of the essential requisites of an orator was held to be that he must be a good man, and that no one may expect to succeed in any calling of life unless he is pure. Say that the knowledge meant is obviously not of earthly things but of the mysteries of God; that in the kindness we trace an effort to reproduce the graciousness held to be a characteristic attribute of God and Christ; and that in the Holy Ghost we may see a reference both to spiritual gifts such as tongues and prophecy and to the impulses and promptings in which the writer traced the Spirit’s general guidance. Note that the love without hypocrisy is the only love worth while. On the word of truth raise a grammatical doubt, since both words are without the article, so that a subjective meaning, a truthful word as distinct from insincerity of speech, is grammatically possible — but a parallel elsewhere gives ample warrant for retaining the objective meaning, the word which conveys God’s truth to men. On the power of God, report that most of the older commentators explain it of the power of working miracles, while holding that it probably includes all the displays of divine power attending the gospel, whether in miracles or in conversions; or elsewhere, distinguishing it from the Spirit just named, judge it natural to refer it chiefly to the supernatural power given for miracles. Divide the armour by hands, offensive weapons on the right and defensive on the left. Then note that the preposition changes from instrument to state or condition, so that it denotes not the means but the medium, the midst of honour and dishonour; play out the prefixes of the two words for report, both of which stand here alone in the New Testament; and add that a later writing expressly describes the apostle in the mouth of his adversaries as a deceiver disseminating deceit, such slander from one’s enemies being praise. And hear in the passage the sensitiveness of a recent experience, a glory not sought and an ignominy not deserved, the very word deceiver, most galling of all to one conscious of his truthfulness, recklessly flung at him.

Take the first words as regarding chiefly the inward man, the exercise of grace and a spiritual behaviour: pureness of doctrine and conversation, chastity of body and mind, sincerity of heart and integrity of life. On the second word, allow that it may be taken in two senses, either as doctrine itself or as skill in acting properly, and prefer the latter. Note that some take the mention of the Spirit to denote spiritual graces, and dismiss as frivolous the inference that the other excellences must be peculiar to the apostle because the Spirit is mentioned separately — as if they were from any other source than the Holy Spirit; the Spirit is named separately as a general term set in the midst of particular instances. Understand the righteousness of the armour as rectitude of conscience and holiness of life, and explain why arms are spoken of at all: all who serve God must fight, inasmuch as the devil is always on the alert to molest them; and they must be completely armed, because if he does not succeed in one onset he makes a new attempt and attacks at one time from before, at another from behind, now on this side and then on that. Then make the last pair the severest test of all: this is no slight test for subjecting a man to trial, for to a man of a noble spirit nothing is more unpleasant than to incur disgrace, and we may observe in all histories that there have been few men of heroism who have not fallen back on being irritated by insults. Hence it is indicative of a mind well established in virtue not to be moved away from one’s course by any disgrace incurred — a rare virtue, but one without which you cannot show that you are a servant of God; we must have a regard to good character, but only so far as the edification of our brethren requires it.

Gloss the first words in order: pureness as simplicity of intention and purity of affection, with the chastity and holiness of life the gospel enjoins; knowledge as knowledge of the divine mysteries; long-suffering as under all provocations; kindness as towards our most virulent persecutors and towards all men. On the Holy Ghost, report that there are doubts among learned men whether the third person of the Trinity is meant or some grace or quality of the soul so denominated, as implying a spirit wholly purified and fitted to be a habitation of God; and quote the rabbinic ladder in which reflection leads to sedulity, sedulity to innocence, innocence to abstinence, abstinence to cleanness, cleanness to sanctity, sanctity to the fear of sin, the fear of sin to humility, humility to piety, and piety to the Holy Spirit. Take the word of truth as the doctrine received immediately from God and faithfully preached to men, and the power of God as confirming that doctrine both by the miracles they were enabled to work and by the application of the truth to the souls of the people by the divine energy. Identify the armour with the whole armour of God described in the other epistle, and assign the pieces: the girdle of truth, the breastplate of righteousness, the shoes of the gospel of peace, the shield of faith, the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit — particularly the shield on the left arm and the sword in the right hand; and call it far-fetched to understand the right hand as signifying prosperity and the left adversity. Elsewhere distinguish the divine prudence from the worldly, since worldly prudence is the practical use of worldly wisdom while divine prudence is the due exercise of grace, making spiritual understanding go as far as possible; call love unfeigned the chief fruit of the Spirit; and divide the last pair by distance, honour and dishonour when we are present, evil report and good report when we are absent — asking who could bear honour and good report were it not balanced by dishonour.

Take the words as a description of the Church rather than of a man. When the first Church was cast off, in the second, which is the Catholic Church, God set first apostles, secondly prophets, thirdly teachers, then miracles, then gifts of healings, helps, governments, divers kinds of tongues, and every sort of virtue — wisdom and understanding, temperance and justice, mercy and loving-kindness, and patience unconquerable in persecutions. She, by the armour of righteousness on the right hand and on the left, by honour and dishonour, in former days amid persecutions and tribulations crowned the holy martyrs with the varied and blooming chaplets of patience, and now in times of peace by God’s grace receives her due honours from kings and those in high place, and from every sort and kindred of men. And while the kings of particular nations have bounds set to their authority, the Holy Church Catholic alone extends her power without limit over the whole world, for God has made her border peace.

debates: Whether pureness here means chastity in particular or integrity in general.
Whether the knowledge is of divine mysteries or practical prudence.
Why the Holy Spirit is named among a list of graces.
Whether the power of God means miracle or every divine working.
What the right hand and the left signify in the armour.
outliers: Ellicott restricts pureness to personal chastity, where Gill, Clarke and Barnes take it broadly.
Calvin and Wesley read the knowledge as practical prudence, against Ellicott and Clarke.
Clarke reports a doubt whether the Holy Ghost here is the third person at all, and quotes a rabbinic ladder ending in the Spirit.
Calvin calls an earlier expositor’s inference from the separate mention of the Spirit frivolous.
Clarke rejects as far-fetched the reading of right and left as prosperity and adversity.
Cyril of Jerusalem applies the whole passage to the Catholic Church and its martyrs rather than to the apostle.
Robertson notes that a later writing puts the word deceiver into the mouth of the apostle’s adversaries.

9.pericope_label: As unknown, and yet well known; as dying, and behold, we live — as sorrowful, yet alway rejoicing; as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, and yet possessing all things

schools.summary: Read the whole series as answers to things actually said, and reconstruct the taunts. Take the word unknown as a jibe at obscure antecedents, since in the absence of fuller information about the disparaging language used it is not easy to fix the precise force, and answer that wherever the writer was known at all he was recognised as being what indeed he was. Hear behind the words about dying a reference partly to the sentence of death already spoken of and partly to the malignant exultation with which that news had been, or was likely to be, received by those who hated him; picture them saying that his course will soon be over and he will not trouble them long, and answer that he is still in full energy, chastened and disciplined but not, as they fondly thought, killed and delivered over unto death. Ask at the word sorrowful whether we are still in the region of taunts and sneers, and whether men said of him what had been said of the saints before him, that he was smitten of God and afflicted, or that when he wept it was turned to his reproof; judge it likeliest that the Jewish rivals, or the jesters of the city, taunted him with a want of cheerfulness, saying he was always in trouble, and set against it the ever-flowing well-spring of a joy that is not of the world but of the Holy Ghost. At the word poor prefer the rendering as a beggar, and suppose that the daily toil at the tent-cloth and the gifts accepted from another church furnished occasion for a taunting jest. Elsewhere reach the first pair by grammar instead: ignored as nonentities, obscure and without proper credentials, and yet fully recognised by all who really matter, a career full of paradox. Take the unknown also of men going as strangers to preach, without introduction from the great or the noble, and turn it into a charge against ministers who, finding themselves among strangers, feel at liberty to lay aside their ministerial character. Explain the sorrow as the world’s estimate of religion, since men who look only on the trials suppose Christians must be always suffering and sad and regard them as among the most unhappy of mortals, joy being thought to belong to the gaieties of this life and sadness to religion — while conceding that they are serious, and that their seriousness is often interpreted as gloom. Say the riches conferred are spiritual. And call the last clause the climax of the whole panegyric on the Christian ministry, observing that the thread of the narrative broken off four chapters earlier is here resumed, and marking the play between the simple verb for having and the compound for holding fast.

Sharpen the first term into suspicion: persons to be suspected of harbouring dark designs, of neither birth, parentage, nor respectable connections in life; and answer it from the record, since they are proved by their whole conduct to have no such designs and are readily traceable from place to place through the whole train of their peregrinations, having preached openly and done nothing in a corner. Press an argument on the chastening that others do not: they continue in the very same line of conduct supposed to bring these chastenings upon them, a course which, if it were criminal, would justly expose them to death for incorrigible obstinacy; and their preservation is itself a proof that they please God. Suppose considerate men judging from the persecuted state and laborious occupation, often destitute of the necessaries of life and scarcely ever enjoying its comforts, that these must be the most miserable of all men — yet they rejoice always, having the consolation of God’s Spirit at all times and a glorious prospect of a blessed immortality. Then argue the enriching materially: the gospel, faithfully preached and fully received, betters the condition of the poor, for it makes them sober, so that they save what before they profusely and riotously spent, and diligent, so that they employ to useful purposes the time they before squandered away; they therefore both save and gain by religion, and these must lead to an increase of property, so that they are made rich, at least in comparison with the sinful and profligate state they were in before. Limit the all things to what is really necessary to the preservation of life, since the wants under which they labour are only for a time. Elsewhere keep it theological, that the world knows them not because it knew him not; make the sorrow internal, for our own manifold imperfections and for the sins and sufferings of our brethren, balanced by present peace and love and power and a sure hope of future glory; and end on the possession, since all things are ours if we are Christ’s — what a magnificence of thought is this.

Locate the ignorance precisely: they are not unknown to the Father, the Son and the Spirit, or to one another, but to the world; and not with respect to their outward estate but their spiritual and eternal state, since the world does not know that they are the chosen of God and born again, and knows neither what life they live nor what they live upon, being unacquainted alike with their inward troubles and with their spiritual joys. Allow that something more may be intended in the word, namely that they were not owned, esteemed or approved, but slighted, despised, hated and persecuted. And note that the sorrow spoken of is a matter of outward appearance.

debates: What the world does not know about the ministers of God.
Whether these clauses answer particular taunts.
What the chastening without killing proves.
Whether the riches conferred on others are spiritual or material.
What is possessed by those who have nothing.
outliers: Ellicott reconstructs the actual words of the opponents behind four separate clauses.
Clarke argues that continued preservation under the same conduct is itself proof of divine approval.
Clarke reads the enriching of others as a real improvement in property; Robertson takes the riches as spiritual.
Robertson marks the close as the climax of the panegyric and the resumption of a narrative broken off four chapters earlier.
Barnes turns the verse into a rebuke of ministers who drop their character among strangers.
Ellicott prefers the rendering beggar to poor, and connects it with the tent-making.

11.pericope_label: O ye Corinthians, our mouth is open unto you, our heart is enlarged — ye are not straitened in us, but ye are straitened in your own bowels

schools.summary: Mark the break: there was manifestly a pause here as the letter was dictated, the rush of thoughts having reached its highest point, so that the writer rests and feels almost as if some apology were needed for so vehement an outpouring of emotion — and nowhere else in the whole range of the epistles do we find any parallel to this form of address. Make the first verb intransitive, a mouth standing open, and take it as the sign that nothing has been kept back in the portrayal of the glory of the ministry, since out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks; note that the verb rendered enlarged occurs in the New Testament only here and where the phylacteries are said to be broadened. Explain the freedom by the affection: the heart was full, and words then flow freely, so that he spoke with the utmost freedom of what he had thought and purposed and done, having loved them so much that he was willing to be reproached and persecuted and poor. Then correct the English of the following verse: the Greek word denotes the upper viscera, the heart, the lungs, the liver, applied by Greek writers to those parts of victims eaten during or after the sacrifice, and hence to the seat of the gentler emotions — whereas our own word is usually applied to the lower viscera and by no means expresses the idea. Make the contrast one of capacity: in that large heart there was room for them and for a thousand others, an infinite elasticity of sympathy, while the narrowness was in their own affections, in hearts so straitened by passions and prejudices and antipathies that they would not make room for him; and suspect a cause, that adversaries may have induced some of them to tighten up their affections. On the last verse, render the noun as a return, expressing reciprocity, and ground the claim in the relation, since children should requite the care and love of parents and these are his spiritual children; observe that the word is unattested outside this passage, one other verse and later Christian writers, so that it was either taken from the vernacular or coined; and note that no verb is expressed to govern the accusative. State also what is not asked: not silver or gold or any earthly possession, but only a return of love and a devotedness to the cause.

Take the open mouth as a sign of boldness, comparing the promise that a prophet should have his mouth opened in the midst of the house of Israel, and the request elsewhere that utterance may be given to speak boldly; and define the enlarged heart as the cheerfulness that springs from benevolence, noting that an eastern expositor takes substantially the same view, since what warms a thing is wont to widen it. Explain the following verse as a reproach: it is owing to their own fault that they cannot share in this cheerfulness, for his mouth is open so that he deals familiarly with them and his very heart would willingly pour itself out, but they shut up their bowels; and it is owing to their corrupt judgment that the things he utters are not relished by them. Offer the alternative sense as well, that they are not brought into straits and difficulties by him, since he does not afflict and distress them. Then soften the reproof by addressing them as sons and by an exhortation which intimates that good hopes are still entertained of them, and explain the recompense as the mutual duty that obtains between a father and his sons: as it is the duty of parents to nourish their children and instruct and defend them, so equity dictates that children should make return. And record that the ancient versions render the clause variously, one having the same recompence, another grant to me the same recompence, and a third turning it into a demand that what is owing be repaid.

Introduce the caution that follows with a profession, in a very pathetic manner, of the most tender affection, like that of a father to his children. Observe that though the apostle was happy in a great fluency of expressions, he yet seemed to want words to express the warm affections he had for these readers, as if he would fain convince them how well he loved them: we are desirous to promote the spiritual and eternal welfare of all to whom we preach, and yet our mouth is open unto you and our heart is enlarged unto you in a special manner. And because his heart was thus enlarged with love to them, therefore he opened his mouth so freely to them in kind admonitions and exhortations, saying that they are not straitened in us, since we would gladly do you all the service we can and promote your comfort, as helpers of your faith and your joy.

Say that the preceding verses contain a very fine specimen of a powerful and commanding eloquence, and that he speaks with the utmost freedom and fluency because of his affection, his heart being expanded to take them and all their interests in and to keep them in the most affectionate remembrance. Take the metaphor of the following verse from a person pent up in a small or narrow place where there is scarcely room to breathe, and say that he has not the same place in their affections which they have in his, the bowels being used in Scripture to denote the most tender affections; their hearts are shut up and so not capable of the blessings they might enjoy. Then make the request small and say so: that they may in some sort repay him for his affection towards them, he speaks to them as to his children whom he has a right to command, and asks nothing hard or grievous but only that they be enlarged — love me as I love you; open your hearts, first to God and then to us, that God may dwell in you and that ye may receive us. Note also that this appellation is seldom used, and that it has here a peculiar force.

Recapitulate before commenting. Having detailed his own trials and afflictions — in patience, in afflictions, in necessities, in distresses, in stripes, in imprisonments, in tumults, in labours, in watchings — and having shown that the thing was a great good, since he is as sorrowful yet always rejoicing, as poor yet making many rich, as having nothing and yet possessing all things; and having called those things armour, and having represented God’s abundant care and power, that the exceeding greatness of the power may be of God and not of us; and having recounted his labours, since we always bear about his dying, which is a clear demonstration of the resurrection, that the life of Jesus may be manifested in our mortal flesh; and having told of what things he was made partaker and with what he had been entrusted, since we are ambassadors on behalf of Christ, as though God were entreating by us — only then let the address by name stand as the climax of all of it.

debates: Why the readers are suddenly addressed by name.
What the opened mouth and the enlarged heart signify.
Whether the narrowness is a fault of judgment or of affection.
What recompense is being asked for.
Whether the English word for the affections renders the Greek.
outliers: Ellicott hears an audible pause in the dictation at this point and says the form of address is without parallel in the epistles.
Barnes objects that the English word for the affections names the wrong organs and does not express the Greek at all.
Robertson finds the noun for recompense unattested outside two verses and later Christian writers.
Calvin cites an eastern expositor as agreeing with him on the enlarged heart.
The editorial matter printed with Calvin supplies a Greek term for filial duty formed from the name of the stork, with an account of the bird.
Chrysostom recapitulates the whole preceding argument before letting the address stand as its climax.

14.pericope_label: Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers — what concord hath Christ with Belial? — ye are the temple of the living God

schools.summary: Say that the apostle particularly speaks of marriage, though the reasons urged hold equally against any needless intimacy, and that of the five questions which follow the three former contain the argument and the two latter the conclusion. Elsewhere deny the marriage reading and make the term military: the verb signifies to leave one’s own rank, place or order and go into another, so that the charge is to keep in your own ranks and not leave the Christian community to join that of the heathen; it must signify not only that they should not join the Gentiles in idolatrous feasts but that they should not apostatise, and the questions that follow show there was a fellowship formed with the heathen both wicked and absurd, which if not checked would infallibly lead to final apostasy. Grant that the exhortation may be applied to the marriages of pious persons with those not decidedly religious, but insist that this is certainly not the meaning here. Then put the incompatibility of temple and idols as a pair of absolutes: nothing could appear more abominable to a Jew than an idol in the temple of God, and the worship of the two is wholly incompatible, since an idolater never worships the true God and a Christian never worships an idol — if ye join in idolatrous rites it is impossible that ye should be Christians. Press the promise of indwelling as emphatic: God intends to make the heart of every believer his own house, and will not be as a wayfaring man who turns aside to tarry for a night, but will take up his constant residence and dwell in and among them. And note that the sentence does not say the temple of idols, for idols do not dwell in their worshippers; that the one verb signifies his perpetual presence and the other his operation; and that the promise to be their God and have them for his people is the sum of the whole gospel covenant.

Trace the transition, which seems abrupt: there was a false latitude as well as a true, and the baser party might think it a matter of indifference whether they married a heathen or chose their intimate friends among the worshippers of Aphrodite — and it is against that kind of enlargement that the protest is entered. Note that the Greek word for the yoking is found nowhere else and was probably coined for the purpose, its meaning determined by the cognate noun in the law forbidding cattle to gender with a diverse kind, and by the prohibition of ploughing with an ox and an ass together; men and women are so yoked when they have no common bond of faith in God, though another explanation refers the image to the yoke of a balance. Report that no other example of the verb has been found; render the present imperative as stop becoming so yoked, which implies that some were already guilty; and hold that marriage is certainly included though other unions may be in mind. Count the five words as they come, fellowship, communion, concord, portion, agreement, and turn one of them on the present day as a pertinent challenge where church members wink at violations of the laws of the land and of God. Take the word for concord musically, since it is used of the unison produced by instruments, so that there is as much discord between Christ and Belial as between instruments producing only jarring sounds. On the name itself, give the literal sense as without profit, worthlessness, wickedness, applied here to Satan, whom the Syriac names outright; note that this is its only occurrence in the New Testament and that it does not appear in the Greek version of the Old at all; that the English version, following the Vulgate, translates the phrase as though it were a proper name; and that this has led to the current belief, as shown in the poems of Milton, that it was the name of a demon or fallen angel, the representative of impurity. Say that mingling with the world would be as absurd as erecting the image of a heathen god in the temple of the Lord, and that the language here can hardly be paralleled in the best classical writers. And observe that the promise which follows is a composite citation drawn from several passages, the opening clause about dwelling in them being found in none of them.

Deny that civil society and converse with unbelievers is forbidden, since that is impracticable and believers must then needs go out of the world, the many natural and civil relations subsisting among men making it necessary, and in many cases lawful and laudable, especially where there is any likelihood of doing them service in a spiritual way; deny too that this dehorts from entering into marriage contracts with such persons, since such marriages were allowed lawful in the former epistle and ought to be abode by — though believers would do well to avoid such a yoke, since it exposes them to many snares and sorrows — for there is nothing in the text or context that leads to that interpretation. Then narrow the fault to idolatry: regaining his authority as a father, he reproves them more freely for associating with unbelievers as partakers in outward idolatry, since imagining nothing unlawful for them in outward things they defiled themselves with wicked superstitions, frequenting the banquets of unbelievers and participating in profane and impure rites, and thinking themselves innocent while they sinned grievously. Note that the matter was censured and exposed at great length in the former epistle, and that since all had not yet been gained over he does not resume it anew but contents himself with a short admonition, as we are accustomed to do with things well known — though his brevity does not prevent his giving sharp cuts. On the name of the adversary, say that the Hebrews themselves are not agreed as to its etymology, reporting the derivations from not profitable and from without yoke, and which of them a later scholar preferred; and list the variant spellings and the three derivations, one making it without ascent, one a man who never succeeds or prospers, one without yoke, that is a breaker of the yoke of God. And ask what association or covenant the saints, who are the temple of God, can have with idols or their worshippers, since the ark of the Lord had none with Dagon, who fell down and was broken before it.

Turn the questions against a heresy: may the Lord deliver us from such delusion, and may there be given you a hatred against the serpent, that as they lie in wait for the heel so you may trample on their head. What agreement can there be between our state and theirs? What communion hath light with darkness? What hath the majesty of the Church to do with the abomination of these men? Here is order, here is discipline, here is majesty, here is purity: here even to look upon a woman to lust after her is condemnation; here is marriage with sanctity, here steadfast continence, here virginity in honour like unto the angels; here is partaking of food with thanksgiving and gratitude to the Creator of the world; here the Father of Christ is worshipped, and fear and trembling are taught before him who sends the rain. Add the exhortation to chastity, whose crown is angelic and whose excellence is above man: be chary of bodies that are to shine as the sun, and do not for short pleasure defile so noble a body, since the sin is short and momentary but the shame is for many years and for ever.

debates: Whether the prohibition concerns marriage, idolatrous feasts, or association generally.
What the coined word for unequal yoking is drawn from.
What the name Belial means and where it comes from.
Whether Belial is a proper name at all.
Where the promise at the end is quoted from.
outliers: Wesley says the apostle particularly speaks of marriage; Clarke and Gill both deny that marriage is meant at all.
Robertson infers from the tense that some of the readers were already guilty.
Ellicott blames the Vulgate and the English version for turning Belial into a proper name, and traces the resulting demon to Milton.
Gill and Calvin between them report five spellings and three incompatible derivations of the same word.
Wesley notes that the text does not say the temple of idols, since idols do not dwell in their worshippers.
Robertson observes that the opening clause of the closing promise occurs in none of the passages it is drawn from.

17.pericope_label: Come out from among them, and be ye separate, saith the Lord — and will be a Father unto you, and ye shall be my sons and daughters

schools.summary: Call the first quotation composite and the second a mosaic of citations, and assign each clause its source, noting that the Greek word rendered Almighty is commonly used in the older version as the equivalent of the Lord of hosts, and that in the New Testament it occurs only here and in one other book. Explain the primary historical sense, that the words were addressed to the priests and Levites who were to return from exile and were not to bring back with them any symbol of the unclean ritual they had witnessed there; then say that this local and historical meaning has passed away for the apostle, and that the unclean thing is identified with the whole system of heathenism. Reconstruct how the passage came to hand: the close connection of this verse with the great prophecy of the atoning work makes it probable that in writing of that work the apostle had remembered, or perhaps actually turned to, the neighbouring chapter as it stood in the Greek version, and so was led on to the verse which almost immediately preceded it. Elsewhere state the principle of citation plainly: the language is not used as though it had original reference to Christians, but is applied as containing an important principle applicable to the case in hand, the writers of the New Testament often using the Old in this manner; and note that the exile city is in Scripture the emblem of whatever is proud, arrogant, wicked and opposed to God. On the promise, say that a father is the protector, counsellor and guide of his children, that no relation is more tender and no rank more elevated than to be adopted into the family of God, and that the most poor and ignorant and despised may reflect that they are the children of the ever-living God and have the Maker of the heavens and the earth as their Father and eternal Friend — how poor are all the honours of the world compared with this. And note the Hebraism in the construction of the last clause.

Report that the Jewish writers usually interpret the summons as a call to come out of captivity and quit the cities and countries where the people were scattered, and that the same words are applied elsewhere to mystical Babylon as a call to God’s people to leave her superstitions and idolatries lest they be partakers of her plagues; take them here as an exhortation to believers in general to forsake the company and conversation of the men of the world. Explain the circumlocution by which the prophet describes the priests, who are named from their charge of the vessels by which the sacrifices and the other parts of divine worship were performed, and observe that his design is to admonish them that while eagerly desiring the day of deliverance they should guard against contamination from the many pollutions with which the country was overrun — and draw the inference, that if so much purity was required of those who carried the vessels, how much more in the vessels themselves, since all our members are set apart for the spiritual worship of God. On the adoption, deny that this is the commencement of the relation or even its first manifestation, which had already been made by the Spirit of adoption witnessing with their spirits, and take it of God’s continuing to act the part of a father: pitying his children, sympathising with them, supporting them under their trials, providing food and raiment, laying up for them in his covenant and in his Son and in heaven, passing by their offences, correcting them for their good, and at last giving them the heavenly inheritance. Then turn the honour into an argument for holiness: a recognition of the great honour to which God has exalted us should stir up a more ardent desire for holiness, since it is no common honour to be reckoned among the sons of God, and it belongs to us in our turn to take care that we do not show ourselves degenerate children — for what injury we do to God if, while we call him father, we defile ourselves with the abominations of idols.

Make the whole promise conditional and say so as a question: is it not plain from this and the following verse that God would be their God only on the ground of their taking him for such, and that this depended on their being separated from the works and workers of iniquity? For God could not inhabit in them if they had concord with Belial or a portion with infidels; and those who will have the promises of God fulfilled to them must come under the conditions of those promises, since if they are not separate, and if they touch the unclean thing, God will not receive them and will not be their God, nor shall they be his people. Propose a re-ordering of the text, holding that the first verse of the chapter following ought to conclude this one, where the same thing is most forcibly stated. On the promise of fatherhood, say that God will act towards them as the most affectionate father can act towards his best beloved child, that they shall be of the household of God and the family of heaven, holy and happy and continually safe. Then measure the promise by the difference between fathers: earthly fathers, however loving and affectionate, may fail to provide for their children because everything is not at their disposal, and they may frequently lack both the power and the means though to will is present with them; but the Lord who made and who governs all things can never lack will, power, nor means, so that the promise is sure to the children — and the children are those who take the Almighty for their God. Elsewhere read the separation as keeping at the utmost distance from the unclean person, and the receiving as a receiving into God’s house and family; apply the promise once made to a king to all believers, as another promise given to a captain is applied to them elsewhere; and ask who can express the worth or conceive the dignity of this divine adoption, which belongs to all who believe the gospel and gives them such free and welcome access as a beloved child has to an indulgent father.

Take the adoption for the theme of a charge to those who are finishing the course of a fast. Be of good courage, O Jerusalem; the Lord will take away all thine iniquities, and will wash away the filth of his sons and of his daughters by the spirit of judgment and by the spirit of burning; he will sprinkle clean water upon you, and ye shall be cleansed from all your sin. Angels shall dance around you and ask who this is that cometh up in white array, leaning upon her beloved; for the soul that was formerly a slave has now adopted her Master himself as her kinsman, and he, accepting the unfeigned purpose, will answer that she is fair. Draw from the figure of the flocks new shorn the confession of a good conscience, and from their bearing twins a twofold grace — that which is perfected of water and of the Spirit, or that which is announced by the Old Testament and by the New. And pray that all of them, when they have finished the course of the fast, may remember what is said and bring forth fruit in good works.

debates: What the summons meant in its original setting.
How the apostle came to have this passage in mind.
Whether the promise is conditional.
What the fatherhood promised adds to what was already true.
Where each clause of the closing promise is drawn from.
outliers: Ellicott reconstructs the apostle turning to a neighbouring chapter of the prophet in the Greek version and being led back one verse.
Barnes states again that the Old Testament words had no original reference to Christians and are applied for their principle.
Clarke makes the promise strictly conditional, and proposes for the second time in this chapter that a verse be moved.
Gill reports the application of the same summons to the church of Rome as mystical Babylon.
Calvin argues from the purity required of those who carried the vessels to the purity required of the vessels themselves.
Clarke measures the divine fatherhood by the failures of earthly fathers who lack the means to provide.
